topic.title: Photobiomodulation or Photorejuvenation, Body Contouring, and Hair Restoration: A Comparative Review of Evidence for Aesthetic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery
topic.abstract: Background: Photobiomodulation (PBM) uses red and near-infrared (NIR) light to induce non-thermal, photochemical effects through mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase activation. Its evidence base in aesthetic surgery has evolved substantially since the last comprehensive plastic surgery review. Objectives: To compare the strength of evidence for PBM in photorejuvenation, body contouring, and hair restoration, and to provide practical recommendations. Methods: A narrative review was conducted in accordance with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles. MEDLINE, EMBASE, EBM Reviews, and Google Scholar were searched through March 2026 for clinical studies, systematic reviews, and consensus statements of red (600-700 nm) and NIR (700-1100 nm) PBM. Levels of evidence followed the hierarchy adopted by the 2025 multidisciplinary Delphi consensus on PBM. Results: Androgenetic alopecia carries the strongest support (Level IA), with meta-analyses reporting density gains of 17 to 24 hairs/cm2, comparable to finasteride in indirect comparisons and topical minoxidil in head-to-head trials. Photorejuvenation carries moderate support (Level IB), as sham-controlled RCTs using objective endpoints have produced inconsistent results. Evidence for body contouring remains limited, with one systematic review of three RCTs reporting modest circumferential reductions and two negative sham-controlled trials. Adverse events were mild and transient. All domains share small sample sizes, manufacturer-funded trials, heterogeneous protocols, and short follow-up. Conclusions: PBM is a safe adjunct within the plastic surgeon's multimodal aesthetic framework, best supported for androgenetic alopecia. Standardized protocols, independent replication, and head-to-head comparisons are needed before broader adoption.
